proposals.description: Telemetry shows a sustained, non-transient rise in coolant_temp_c from 90°C to 114°C over ~2 hours, tightly correlated with a steady drop in coolant_level_pct from 96% to 76%. Oil pressure and RPM remained normal/stable throughout, indicating the trend is not an engine-load artifact. KB search returned two conflicting entries: KB-001 attributes coolant spikes to a transient sensor calibration glitch (fix: restart_sensor) with no real temperature change, while KB-002 attributes sustained spikes correlated with falling coolant level to a genuine leak/coolant loss (fix: schedule_service_visit). The observed data matches KB-002's pattern (sustained, correlated with real coolant loss) rather than KB-001's (transient, no real change), so a physical inspection for a coolant leak is warranted rather than a sensor restart.

KB search returned two conflicting entries: KB-001 attributes coolant spikes to a transient sensor calibration glitch (fix: restart_sensor), while KB-002 attributes sustained spikes correlated with falling coolant level to a genuine leak (fix: schedule_service_visit). Telemetry shows a sustained, monotonic rise in coolant_temp_c from 90°C to 114°C over 2 hours, tightly correlated with coolant_level_pct dropping from 96% to 76% -- not a transient blip. Oil pressure and RPM remained stable, ruling out other causes. This matches KB-002's conditions, indicating real coolant loss requiring physical inspection rather than a sensor fault.

Telemetry shows a sustained, monotonic coolant temp rise (88.5°C→114°C over 90 min) tightly correlated with falling coolant level (96%→76%), while oil pressure and RPM remained normal. KB-001 and KB-002 disagree: KB-001 says spikes can be a transient sensor glitch (fix: restart_sensor) with no real correlation to level; KB-002 says a sustained spike correlated with low coolant level indicates a genuine leak/coolant loss requiring inspection (fix: schedule_service_visit). The observed data matches KB-002's pattern (sustained, not transient, and clearly correlated with level drop), not KB-001's. Recommend scheduling a service visit to inspect for a coolant leak.

Telemetry shows cabin_temp_c drifting from 1.8°C to 5.8°C over 3 hours while controller_reading_c stayed flat at 1.8-2.2°C (matching the 2°C setpoint) the entire time, and compressor current fell from ~11.9A to ~8.2A as the controller throttled cooling believing it was on-target. KB-003 describes two possible causes for temperature drift: (a) controller sensor calibration drift, where the controller reading stays at setpoint while actual cabin temp diverges -- fixed via send_diagnostic_reset; or (b) a refrigeration circuit fault, where the controller reading tracks the cabin probe and both rise together -- requiring a technician visit. The telemetry matches scenario (a), not (b), since the controller reading never tracked the rising cabin temperature. No prior service history complicates this further. Recommending the diagnostic reset per KB-003's calibration-drift branch.

Telemetry shows cabin_temp_c climbing steadily from 2.0°C to 5.6°C over 4 hours while controller_reading_c stays flat around 2.0°C (matching setpoint) and compressor_current_a actually declines (11.5A→8.2A), indicating the compressor is throttling back because the controller believes setpoint is satisfied. This matches KB-003's first pattern exactly: cabin drifts above setpoint while the controller's own return-air reading still shows setpoint, pointing to sensor calibration drift rather than a refrigeration circuit fault. KB-003's alternate condition (controller reading tracking the cabin probe, implying a hardware/circuit fault needing a technician) does not hold here since the two readings diverge. Per KB-003, the recommended fix for this calibration-drift pattern is a remote diagnostic reset to re-run controller self-calibration. No prior service history exists for this unit to suggest a recurring hardware issue.

Telemetry shows cabin_temp_c climbing steadily from 2.0°C to 5.6°C over 2 hours while controller_reading_c stays flat and oscillating around the 2°C setpoint (1.8-2.2°C), and compressor_current_a is tapering down from 11.5A to ~8.2A as the controller throttles cooling believing setpoint is met. This matches KB-003: controller's own return-air reading still tracks setpoint while actual cabin temp drifts above it, indicating sensor calibration drift causing under-cooling (not a refrigeration circuit fault, which would show controller reading tracking the rising cabin probe). No conflicting KB entries were found, and no prior service history exists for this unit. Recommended fix is a remote diagnostic reset to re-run controller self-calibration.

Telemetry shows oil pressure steadily declining from 35.7 psi to ~18 psi over ~90 minutes, then plateauing near 18-19 psi while coolant temp (88-90°C) and RPM (1600-1700) stayed normal — indicating a genuine, sustained low-pressure condition rather than sensor noise or an overheating-driven artifact. Only one relevant KB entry (KB-004) was found, so there is no conflicting guidance: it states low oil pressure warnings on diesel engines are not resolved by sensor restart and require a service visit. Service history shows the oil pressure sensor was already replaced in March for an unrelated fault, further supporting a real mechanical cause (e.g., pump wear, leak, or low oil level) rather than sensor fault. Recommending scheduling a service visit.

The observed pattern matches KB-001 (isolated single-point spike, stable coolant level) rather than KB-002 (which requires sustained elevation plus level loss), so restart_sensor is the appropriate fix. KB has two conflicting entries: KB-001 (transient sensor glitch, no real temp rise) vs KB-002 (sustained spike + low coolant level = real leak, needs service visit). Recommending sensor restart; if spikes recur or coolant level drops, escalate to service visit per KB-002.

proposals.description: Telemetry shows stable compressor operation (~11-12A) until 20:10, when current spiked to 24A (2x normal), then dropped to 0A at 20:20 with compressor_state locking into 'fault' for the remainder of the window while cabin_temp_c and controller_reading_c climb together from 2.0C to 3.9C (unit no longer cooling). Controller and cabin readings track identically throughout, which per KB-003 rules out a sensor-calibration issue (that fix, diagnostic reset, explicitly does not apply when readings track together) and instead points to the refrigeration circuit/compressor hardware itself. No KB entry directly documents this overcurrent-then-zero-current trip pattern, so this is not a fully documented match -- the overcurrent spike followed by a persistent fault lockout is consistent with a mechanical/electrical compressor fault (e.g., locked rotor, contactor or winding failure) that requires physical technician inspection rather than a remote reset or sensor restart. Recommend a service visit; confidence kept moderate given the lack of a directly matching KB entry.

This pattern (overcurrent spike -> hard lockout -> real loss of cooling) indicates a genuine electrical/mechanical compressor fault (e.g., overload trip, possible locked rotor or contactor issue) rather than a sensor or controller glitch, since the resulting temperature rise is physically consistent with the compressor actually being off. A physical inspection/service visit is the cautious choice given the lack of documented fix and the hardware-fault signature.
